card_summary: The revelation that CDN Netskrt discloses network capacity and revenue should prompt media engineers to reevaluate their egress costs and API orchestration strategies. In practice, this means that cloud-based CDNs are no longer opaque black boxes, and engineers can now make more informed decisions about object storage (S3) and microservices architectures that integrate with their content management systems (MAM). For engineering teams, the real challenge is optimizing storage costs while ensuring data integrity and scalability. In practice, this means that engineering teams will need to balance the cost savings of cloud-based CDNs with the risk of increased egress costs for large-scale media workflows. The trade-off here is between the flexibility of cloud-based infrastructure and the predictability of on-premises storage costs. As media engineers, we should be prepared to adapt our workflows to accommodate the changing economics of cloud-based CDNs, and to prioritize scalability and data integrity in our architecture designs.
body_html:
Why Cloud-Native Storage Is Forcing Broadcasters to Rethink Scalability

Broadcasters are facing a perfect storm of increasing content demand, shrinking budgets, and the need for faster content delivery. The pressure to scale infrastructure without breaking the bank is mounting, and traditional storage solutions are no longer up to the task. As a result, cloud-native storage is emerging as a game-changer for broadcasters looking to future-proof their operations.

What This Development Actually Means

Netskrt, a leading CDN provider, has recently disclosed its network capacity, revenue, and strategies for adding capacity profitably. This move is significant because it highlights the growing importance of scalability in the CDN market. By sharing its approach to scaling, Netskrt is providing a roadmap for other CDNs and broadcasters looking to optimize their infrastructure.

This announcement sits within a broader industry trend towards cloud-native infrastructure and software-defined storage. As broadcasters increasingly adopt cloud-based workflows, the need for scalable storage solutions that can keep pace with growing content demands is becoming more pressing.

Why It Matters for Broadcast Operations

The implications of cloud-native storage for broadcast operations are significant. With the ability to scale storage capacity on demand, broadcasters can reduce their capital expenditures (CapEx) and operating expenses (OpEx) associated with traditional storage solutions. This, in turn, allows them to allocate more resources to content creation and distribution. For example, by leveraging cloud-native storage, broadcasters can reduce their egress costs associated with data transfer and eliminate manual quality control (QC) efforts.

Real-world vendors like Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Microsoft Azure Blob Storage are already providing scalable storage solutions that can meet the demands of cloud-native workflows. These solutions are often integrated with microservices-based architectures and Kubernetes orchestration, enabling broadcasters to deploy and manage their infrastructure with greater flexibility and efficiency.

Impact by Stakeholder

  • Regional and national broadcasters: Will need to budget for scalable storage solutions that can keep pace with growing content demands. By leveraging cloud-native storage, they can reduce their CapEx and OpEx associated with traditional storage solutions and allocate more resources to content creation and distribution.
  • OTT and streaming platforms: Will benefit from the ability to scale storage capacity on demand, reducing their egress costs associated with data transfer and eliminating manual QC efforts. This will enable them to deliver high-quality content to their audiences more efficiently and cost-effectively.
  • Post-production and MAM teams: Will experience workflow implications as broadcasters adopt cloud-native storage solutions. This may include changes to ingest, QC, archive, and content operations, as well as the need to integrate with new storage solutions and APIs.

Analysis: Netskrt's disclosure of its network capacity and revenue is a welcome transparency, but it also reveals a hidden risk: the increasing reliance on CDNs to offload OTT traffic will lead to a surge in SSAI (Server-Side Ad Insertion) adoption, which may compromise the quality of low-latency, low-bandwidth ST 2110 streams.
